Learning Dynamics of Chain-of-Thought State Tracking in a Solvable Transformer Model

Niklas Forner    Marcel Kühn    Matthias Thamm    and Affiliation: Institute for Theoretical Physics, University of Leipzig, D-04103 Leipzig    Bernd Rosenow Affiliation: Institute for Theoretical Physics, University of Leipzig, D-04103 Leipzig Affiliation: ScaDS.AI Dresden/Leipzig, University of Leipzig, D-04105 Leipzig
Abstract

Chain-of-thought generation can turn a multi-step computation into a sequence of locally checkable state updates, but the training dynamics by which transformers acquire such updates remain poorly understood. We study this question in a solvable setting: a simplified one-block transformer trained by supervised next-token prediction on state sequences generated by composing permutations. The architecture separates fixed-lag action retrieval, learned by RoPE attention, from a specialized MLP logic module that applies the retrieved permutation to the current state. Using a statistical-physics mean-field description, we derive closed dynamics for three order parameters measuring attention retrieval, teacher-matrix alignment, and off-target logic overlap. These equations quantitatively match simulations for the order parameters and, combined with a logit-distribution approximation, qualitatively predict the sharp transition in final rollout accuracy. The analysis reveals staged learning: the logic module first learns a mixed heuristic; attention then locks onto the relevant action, enabling efficient MLP alignment. Together, these results provide a controlled mechanistic account of how attention-based retrieval and MLP-based logic co-develop during chain-of-thought state tracking.

1 Introduction

Transformers [1] are highly successful across tasks such as translation, text classification, and question answering [2, 3, 4, 5]. In particular, chain-of-thought reasoning [6] has been a major recent advance: by inserting intermediate tokens that support step-wise answer production, large language models (LLMs) substantially improve on complex tasks [6]. Alongside in-context learning [7, 8, 9, 10] and grokking [11], the sharp performance gain from chain-of-thought reasoning can be viewed as an emergent phenomenon. This performance has motivated much work in explainable AI [12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20], since the internal processes of transformers and LLMs are highly complex. To understand why these systems perform so well, researchers have analyzed them empirically and investigated simplified settings analytically. Prior work [14, 13, 21] suggests that the attention block and multi-layer perceptron (MLP) inside a transformer serve two core functions: attention is mainly responsible for semantic and positional structure, while the MLP largely handles information storage and processing [14, 13, 21]. Of course, these two mechanisms do not have completely separate roles; they depend on each other, and their learning dynamics are coupled during training. This raises basic questions: how do attention and MLP influence one another during training, and when do they learn relative to each other?

In this work, we disentangle these two core parts of a transformer. We let the attention mechanism handle positional information, deliberately without semantic complexity, and let the subsequent MLP act as an information storage and logic module. As a specific problem, we employ a state-tracking task in which the model sequentially composes permutations. This compositional task has been used before to study length generalization of chain-of-thought computation in regular transformers [22]. Due to its exact, discrete nature and its local state dependence on the prior tokens, this task is well suited for detailed analysis. The sequential application of group elements is a problem that can be solved by transformers [23, 20, 22], and in fact by a one-block transformer. Here, we study this problem in a student-teacher setup, through the lens of permutation composition, where an exact teacher is known. By fixing selected parts of the architecture of a one-block transformer, we obtain a solvable model that separates positional retrieval from logical composition learning. In doing so, we study a controlled mechanistic model of serial state tracking via intermediate tokens. Our goal is not to model natural-language chain-of-thought reasoning in full-scale language models. We instead isolate the core of algorithmic chain-of-thought tasks: retrieving an operation from context and applying it to an evolving state. Fixed embeddings and values, together with the specialized MLP-style logic module, are deliberate simplifications that make the retrieval-logic coupling analytically tractable. The resulting model should therefore be read as a solvable mechanistic model of chain-of-thought state tracking, rather than as a complete model of standard transformer reasoning.

Main results and contributions.

(1) We study a specialized, solvable transformer model in which attention learns positional information and an MLP-style block learns a permutation-composition task. (2) We describe the learning process with three order parameters and derive differential equations for their training dynamics. (3) During training, the model first learns a mixed heuristic in the MLP block; later, attention learns the relevant positional retrieval while the MLP logic aligns with the teacher. (4) We model the steep increase in final rollout accuracy, giving a simple explanation for a rapid emergent change as a function of training time.

2 Related work

Explainable AI.

Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand neural networks by reverse-engineering the algorithms they implement [12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20]. Prior work has identified different roles for attention, which performs contextual mapping, and the MLP, which performs value mapping [14]. Some works consider attention-only transformers [12, 16], while others investigate factual knowledge stored in MLP layers [21]. Geva et al. [15] show that feed-forward layers in transformer-based language models operate as key-value memories [24]. Neo et al. [13] analyze interactions between MLP and attention layers and find that some attention heads identify context cues relevant to next-token prediction and, in response, activate downstream neurons that support that prediction.

Analytical models for transformers and limiting cases.

A range of theoretical transformer models and limiting cases has been studied. Poc-López and Aguilera [25] employ a dynamical mean-field approximation for large self-attention networks by mapping attention to an asymmetric Hopfield network [26]. Maloney et al. [27] study a solvable statistical model combining a generative data model and a random feature model, in order to derive neural scaling laws. In-context learning is studied by Lu et al. [28] using a simplified linear self-attention model.

Yang et al. [29] analyze gradient-flow training of a shallow transformer on word co-occurrence recognition and identify a two-phase dynamic in which a linear MLP first aligns with task-relevant target signals while softmax attention remains nearly static; later, attention and MLP jointly increase the margin and drive the loss toward its minimum. Chen and Luo [30] similarly argue for staged transformer optimization in a linearized setting, showing that attention parameters first condense toward task-relevant directions before key–query matrices participate more actively and normalized weights collapse toward low rank. Another transition appears in induction-head formation, where training moves from a "lazy” local nn-gram strategy to a richer in-context mechanism; this again suggests that distinct transformer submodules may enter the learned computation at different points in training [31]. Our work is complementary: rather than analyzing co-occurrence, rank collapse, or induction heads in isolation, we study a chain-of-thought state-tracking task in which the model must maintain and update a latent state across steps. We pair finite-width training runs with analytical predictions that expose a two-stage division of labor between attention-mediated action access and MLP-mediated logical update.

Empirical studies on attention and MLP dynamics.

Tian et al. [32] study joint MLP/attention dynamics in multilayer transformers and report that MLP nonlinearity and residual structure shape how attention evolves during training, supporting the view that feed-forward and attention modules interact rather than learn independently. Chen et al. [33] provide an empirical parallel: in a controlled next-token prediction setting, feed-forward layers preferentially learn simple distributional associations such as bigrams, whereas attention layers are more closely tied to in-context reasoning. This is consistent with a temporal and functional separation between early MLP learning and later attention-mediated computation. Hakimi et al. [34] find a progression from general-purpose components to specialized factual components at larger model scale, with FFNs remaining comparatively stable and attention heads showing higher turnover. Their results likewise suggest staged component specialization rather than uniform co-development.

Reasoning theory and chain of thought.

Recent progress in LLM reasoning has been facilitated by the observation that transformers often solve complex tasks better when they are allowed to proceed step by step [35]. Chain-of-thought reasoning can produce a qualitative jump in reasoning performance [6]. Transformers are capable of in-context learning [36], and intermediate steps can also help models improve their outputs iteratively [37]. Prystawski et al. [38] investigate how chain-of-thought reasoning improves output quality and show that intermediate steps are helpful when the training data consist of overlapping, strongly interacting local clusters of variables. Although transformers can learn some reasoning tasks using far fewer layers than the number of reasoning steps [39], they cannot learn certain arithmetic tasks without scaling the depth super-polynomially with input size [40]. Nadgir et al. [41] model chain-of-thought reasoning as a tree process and identify a critical branching-degree threshold: below this threshold, reasoning hurts performance, while above it, an optimal tree depth minimizes error. Interestingly, constant-depth transformers can learn serial problems such as permutation composition through chain of thought [42, 40].

Permutation models and permutation composition.

Many tasks require compositions of operations, whether mathematical, algorithmic, or otherwise. The solvability of such sequential group-composition tasks depends on layer depth and architecture [23]. Chughtai et al. [20] investigate how small networks encode finite group operations. Liu et al. [39] show that some composition tasks may be implemented efficiently by the model using shortcuts. This matters because a network may solve the training task while failing to learn the underlying rule, and hence fail to generalize. In this work, we study a state-tracking task in which we can directly follow which state the network is tracking at every step, leaving little room for hidden shortcuts.

Prior work on chain-of-thought and permutation/group-composition tasks primarily addresses expressivity, learnability, length generalization, or reverse engineering of trained circuits. In contrast, our focus is the gradient dynamics by which a transformer-like architecture separates the computation into retrieval and state-update components. The main question is not whether the task can be solved, but how attention and the MLP-style logic module co-evolve during learning, and why final rollout accuracy undergoes a sharp transition.

3 Problem and network setup

To isolate the model’s ability to track latent states, we construct a synthetic environment that serves as a symbolic chain of thought. It retains the core difficulty of serial reasoning: a sequence of intermediate steps must be carried out before the final answer is reached. This yields a teacher with exact state tracking and a student trained to reproduce the resulting chain.

3.1 Permutation-chain task

Consider the first N≥2N\geq 2 positive integers [N]:={1,…,N}[N]:=\{1,\dots,N\} and fix dg≤N!d_{g}\leq N! permutations {σi}i=1,…,dg⊆SN\{\sigma_{i}\}_{i=1,\dots,d_{g}}\subseteq S_{N} acting on [N][N]. This subset forms the action vocabulary for the task. We encode a sequence of permutations, called actions, and the resulting states as a chain of tokens that the network must reproduce. First, we draw L∈ℕL\in\mathbb{N} actions (i.i.d.) from {σi}i=1,…,dg\{\sigma_{i}\}_{i=1,\dots,d_{g}} and represent them by their corresponding indices g1,…,gL∈{1,…,dg}g_{1},\dots,g_{L}\in\{1,\dotsc,d_{g}\}. Second, we choose an initial state s0∈[N]s_{0}\in[N]. Third, we recursively generate LL states by applying the actions in chain form:

st=σgt(st−1),t=1,…,L.s_{t}=\sigma_{g_{t}}(s_{t-1}),\qquad t=1,\dots,L. (1)

This trajectory is concatenated into a single token sequence of total length 2​L+12L+1:

x1=g1,…,xL=gL,xL+1=s0,xL+2=s1,…,x2​L+1=sL.x_{1}=g_{1},\ \dots\ ,\ x_{L}=g_{L},\quad x_{L+1}=s_{0},\quad x_{L+2}=s_{1},\ \dots\ ,\ x_{2L+1}=s_{L}. (2)

Given the actions and the initial state, the student is tasked with generating the LL subsequent states, ending with the final rollout token sLs_{L}. Thus, at inference, the prompt is the prefix (g1,…,gL,s0)(g_{1},\dots,g_{L},s_{0}) and the output is the generated suffix (s1,…,sL)(s_{1},\dots,s_{L}). This chain can be generalized to the sequential application of group elements [23]. Here, we focus on permutations, since they admit an exact matrix representation.

3.2 Network setup

We consider a minimal one-block transformer in a student-teacher setting, in which a modified attention head retrieves the relevant action at a fixed lag and passes it to an explicit logic module. This logic module performs the next-token prediction, thereby isolating retrieval from application. A single-layer transformer can encode the solution [22]; we use this minimal depth to focus on the reasoning process through intermediate steps. Figure 1 summarizes the setup: the chosen permutations determine the teacher sequence, and the student predicts each next token by combining attention-based retrieval with the logic block.

The attention head

We use a single attention head to retrieve the relevant action from the prefix. We choose Rotary Positional Encoding (RoPE) [43] and fix the values in order to focus on positional information. Compared with absolute positional encodings, relative or rotary encodings have been found to perform better [44]. We define

𝐪𝐢\displaystyle\mathbf{q_{i}} :=RoPEi​(WQ​𝐮𝐢)∈ℝdh,𝐤𝐣:=RoPEj​(WK​𝐮𝐣)∈ℝdh,𝐯𝐣:=Val⁡(xj)∈ℝdg,\displaystyle:=\mathrm{RoPE}_{i}\!\left(W_{Q}\,\mathbf{u_{i}}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}}\ ,\quad\mathbf{k_{j}}:=\mathrm{RoPE}_{j}\!\left(W_{K}\,\mathbf{u_{j}}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}}\ ,\quad\mathbf{v_{j}}:=\mathrm{Val}(x_{j})\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{g}}\ , (3)

where dgd_{g} is the size of the action vocabulary, dhd_{h} is the head dimension, and 𝐮𝐢\mathbf{u_{i}} is the embedding of token xix_{i}. The values are defined as one-hot features for action tokens and as zero for state tokens, i.e., Val⁡(gj)=𝐞^𝐠𝐣∈ℝdg\mathrm{Val}(g_{j})=\mathbf{\hat{e}_{g_{j}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{g}} for an action and Val⁡(xj)=𝟎\mathrm{Val}(x_{j})=\mathbf{0} otherwise. To isolate positional information from semantic structure, we hold the embedding vectors fixed at 𝐮𝐢=E⁡(xi)=1∈ℝ1\mathbf{u_{i}}=E(x_{i})=1\in\mathbb{R}^{1} for all i=1,…,2​L+1i=1,\dotsc,2L+1, which reduces the key and query matrices to vectors. Appendix C explains how this can be achieved with bundled embeddings and matrix-shaped keys and queries. Causal attention entries and the attention-head output are given by

πi​j=softmaxj≤min⁡{i,L}​(𝐪𝐢⊤​𝐤𝐣dh),𝐨𝐢:=∑j≤iπi​j​𝐯𝐣.\displaystyle\pi_{ij}=\mathrm{softmax}_{j\leq\min\{i,L\}}\biggl(\frac{\mathbf{q_{i}^{\top}}\mathbf{k_{j}}}{\sqrt{d_{h}}}\biggr),\qquad\mathbf{o_{i}}:=\sum_{j\leq i}\pi_{ij}\,\mathbf{v_{j}}\ . (4)

This dgd_{g}-dimensional output assigns a weight to each possible action. Perfect learning corresponds to a one-hot output identifying the correct action among all dgd_{g} possibilities.

Positional encoding

We apply RoPE to queries and keys, i.e., there are no explicit learned positional embeddings. Let the query/key head dimension be dh∈2​ℕd_{h}\in 2\mathbb{N}; then the encoding is realized by a matrix with dh/2d_{h}/2 planar rotation blocks. RoPE at sequence position ii is the linear map RoPEi​(𝐖):=Ω​(i)​𝐖\mathrm{RoPE}_{i}(\mathbf{W}):=\Omega(i)\,\mathbf{W}, where 𝐖\mathbf{W} is a query or key vector and Ω⁡(i)\Omega(i) is the matrix of block rotations. For attention, the relevant quantities are the query-key dot products. They obey the identity

(RoPEi​(𝐖𝐐))⊤​(RoPEj​(𝐖𝐊))=𝐖𝐐⊤​Ω​(j−i)​𝐖𝐊.\displaystyle\big(\mathrm{RoPE}_{i}(\mathbf{W_{Q}})\big)^{\top}\big(\mathrm{RoPE}_{j}(\mathbf{W_{K}})\big)=\mathbf{W_{Q}^{\top}}\,\Omega(j-i)\mathbf{W_{K}}\ . (5)

The attention matrix therefore depends on the relative offset j−ij-i in the token sequence, which makes RoPE suitable for a fixed-lag retrieval task.

The logic module

The attention output is supplied to a logic module to produce a prediction of the next state. The module can be constructed as a constrained instantiation of a GLU-style MLP; see Appendix C for the explicit construction. It is convenient to represent the permutations by matrices. Applying a permutation can then be written as O⁡(σa)​𝐞𝐣=𝐞σ𝐚​(𝐣)O(\sigma_{a})\,\mathbf{e_{j}}=\mathbf{e_{\sigma_{a}(j)}} for j∈[N],a∈[dg]j\in[N],\ a\in[d_{g}], where {𝐞𝐣}j=1N\{\mathbf{e_{j}}\}_{j=1}^{N} is the standard basis of ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N}.

We introduce the set {Ma}a=1dg\{M_{a}\}_{a=1}^{d_{g}} of learnable matrices Ma∈ℝN×NM_{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}. With attention outputs 𝐨𝐢∈ℝdg\mathbf{o_{i}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{g}}, define the linear map

M~i:=∑a=1dg(oi)a​Ma∈ℝN×N.\tilde{M}_{i}:=\sum_{a=1}^{d_{g}}(o_{i})_{a}\,M_{a}\ \in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}\ . (6)

When the student has learned, this map approximates the correct permutation matrix. Before convergence, it is a weighted sum of the learnable matrices associated with the action vocabulary. Actions identified by the attention head as relevant receive larger weights than irrelevant ones. The next-token computation is performed by matrix multiplication and uses a one-hot encoding of the states. We represent the current state xi=si−L−1x_{i}=s_{i-L-1} as an NN-dimensional one-hot vector 𝐞𝐬𝐢−𝐋−𝟏∈ℝN\mathbf{e_{s_{i-L-1}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} and define 𝐳𝐢+𝟏:=M~i​𝐞𝐬𝐢−𝐋−𝟏∈ℝN\mathbf{z_{i+1}}:=\tilde{M}_{i}\,\mathbf{e_{s_{i-L-1}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}. The prediction is obtained by choosing the index of the maximal entry. We denote the prediction by s^i−L\hat{s}_{i-L}.

This setup preserves the core functionalities of a standard transformer block consisting of an attention head followed by an MLP. During training, the model sees every intermediate token. At inference time, it is given only the prefix (g1,…,gL,s0)(g_{1},\dots,g_{L},s_{0}) and must generate s1,…,sLs_{1},\dots,s_{L}; the final answer is the last generated token sLs_{L}. In this way, the student must carry out a chain-of-thought process to arrive at the last state. Under teacher forcing, the previous state token is locally available and need not be retrieved by a separate transport head. A more general model could include a second attention head tasked with copying this previous state token. In the teacher-forced regime, the current state is already available at the predictor token, so a single nontrivial fixed-lag retrieval for gtg_{t} suffices.

3.3 Teacher model

We specify a teacher within the same architecture that implements the correct dynamics st=σgt​(st−1)s_{t}=\sigma_{g_{t}}(s_{t-1}). To distinguish teacher from student parameters θ\theta, we denote teacher parameters by θ⋆\theta^{\star}.

Attention.

We want the action head to attend from predictor positions j+Lj+L to action positions jj, i.e., to the relative offset −L-L. This corresponds to πj+L,j⋆=1\pi_{j+L,j}^{\star}=1 for j=1,…,Lj=1,\dots,L and zero everywhere else, and can be realized arbitrarily well by an appropriate choice of keys and queries. Then, the attention-head output is 𝐨𝐢⋆=𝐯𝐢−𝐋≡𝐞^𝐠𝐢−𝐋\mathbf{o^{\star}_{i}}=\mathbf{v_{i-L}}\equiv\mathbf{\hat{e}_{g_{i-L}}}, using the same value map as for the student.

Next tokens.

In the teacher logic module, the matrices are set to the exact permutation matrices, Ma⋆:=O⁡(σa)∈ℝN×NM_{a}^{\star}:=O(\sigma_{a})\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} for a=1,…,dga=1,\dots,d_{g}. Consequently, the per-step map becomes M~i⋆=Mgi−L⋆\tilde{M}_{i}^{\star}=M_{g_{i-L}}^{\star} and hence equals the exact permutation matrix Mgi−L⋆=O⁡(σgi−L)M_{g_{i-L}}^{\star}=O(\sigma_{g_{i-L}}). Therefore, the teacher specifies the next token 𝐩𝐢+𝟏⋆=O⁡(σgi−L)​𝐞𝐬𝐢−𝐋−𝟏=𝐞𝐬𝐢−𝐋\mathbf{p_{i+1}^{\star}}=O(\sigma_{g_{i-L}})\,\mathbf{e_{s_{i-L-1}}}=\mathbf{e_{s_{i-L}}} as the analog of the student logit, the target vector. The position of the maximal entry is the correct next state si−Ls_{i-L}.

3.4 Training objective

We train the model autoregressively with teacher forcing on full sequences (2), but compute the loss only on the suffix state tokens s1,…,sLs_{1},\dots,s_{L} (s1=x(L+1)+1,…,sL=x2​L+1s_{1}=x_{(L+1)+1},\dots,s_{L}=x_{2L+1}). We use the cross-entropy loss

ℒ(θ)=⟨1L∑i=L+12​L−logP(xi+1∣x1,…,xi)⟩x1,…,x2​L+1\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\Biggl\langle\frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=L+1}^{2L}-\log P\!\left(x_{i+1}\mid x_{1},\dots,x_{i}\right)\Biggr\rangle_{x_{1},\dots,x_{2L+1}} (7)

with θ\theta denoting the network parameters. The current state token xj+L=sj−1x_{j+L}=s_{j-1} is used to predict the next token. To do so, the model needs the corresponding action token xj=gjx_{j}=g_{j} to apply inside the logic module. The required relative offset is therefore j−(j+L)=−Lj-(j+L)=-L, a single fixed lag independent of the current position. The model performs this next-token prediction at all LL state positions. For the hyperparameters used in simulations, the reader is referred to Table 1 in the appendix. Details on dataset generation are given in Appendix B.

4 Macroscopic order parameters and mean-field formulation

4.1 Order parameters

Attention order parameter

At prediction positions i=L+1,…,2​Li=L+1,\dots,2L, the fixed-lag structure identifies a unique correct action position, namely i−Li-L. We therefore define

A:=1L​∑i=L+12​Lπi,i−L.\displaystyle A:=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=L+1}^{2L}\pi_{i,i-L}\ . (8)

This order parameter measures how much attention mass the head assigns, on average, to the correct action across all prediction steps. Because the attention entries are normalized, A=1A=1 corresponds to perfect attention: at each step, the model retrieves the correct action. When A≈0A\approx 0, the model actively avoids the correct action. Up to fluctuations, A=1/LA=1/L corresponds to random guessing over the LL candidate action positions.

Logic order parameters

Recall the student and teacher matrices {Ma}a=1dg\{M_{a}\}_{a=1}^{d_{g}} and {Ma⋆}a=1dg\{M_{a}^{\star}\}_{a=1}^{d_{g}}. Let

R\displaystyle R :=1dg​∑a=1dg1N​Tr⁡[(Ma⋆)⊤​Ma],\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{d_{g}}\sum_{a=1}^{d_{g}}\frac{1}{N}\Tr\Bigl[\bigl(M^{\star}_{a}\bigr)^{\top}M_{a}\Bigr]\ , (9a)
S\displaystyle S :=1dg​(dg−1)​∑a=1dg∑b=1b≠adg1N​Tr⁡[(Ma⋆)⊤​Mb].\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{d_{g}(d_{g}-1)}\sum_{a=1}^{d_{g}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b=1\\ b\neq a\end{subarray}}^{d_{g}}\frac{1}{N}\Tr\Bigl[(M^{\star}_{a})^{\top}M_{b}\Bigr]\ . (9b)

RR measures the alignment between the student’s learned matrices and the corresponding teacher permutation matrices. SS quantifies the off-target overlap between learned matrices and the other teacher permutation matrices.

4.2 Mean-field loss and logits

Denoting the model-output pre-activations as 𝐳𝐢+𝟏\mathbf{z_{i+1}} at position ii, the cross-entropy loss is given by ℒ=1L∑i=L+12​L[−𝐩𝐢+𝟏⋆⋅𝐳𝐢+𝟏+ln(∑r=1Nezi+1,r)]\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=L+1}^{2L}[-\mathbf{p^{\star}_{i+1}}\cdot\,\mathbf{z_{i+1}}+\ln(\sum_{r=1}^{N}\mathrm{e}^{z_{i+1,r}})]. Here, the teacher specification 𝐩𝐢+𝟏⋆\mathbf{p^{\star}_{i+1}} singles out the correct logit. To obtain an ensemble description, we replace the seed-specific loss by an ensemble-averaged one. We make a mean-field ansatz and replace the correct and other logits by their expectation values with respect to states and actions. The resulting mean-field loss is

ℓCE\displaystyle\ell_{\mathrm{CE}} :=1L∑i=L+12​L−⟨zi+1,k⟩+ln(e⟨zi+1,k⟩+(N−1)e⟨zi+1,k¯⟩),\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=L+1}^{2L}-\langle z_{i+1,k}\rangle+\ln\biggl(\mathrm{e}^{\langle z_{i+1,k}\rangle}+(N-1)\mathrm{e}^{\langle z_{i+1,\overline{k}}\rangle}\biggr)\ , (10)

where the correct logit is denoted by zi+1,k=𝐩𝐢+𝟏⋆⋅𝐳𝐢+𝟏z_{i+1,k}=\mathbf{p_{i+1}^{\star}}\cdot\mathbf{z_{i+1}}. By symmetry, the other logits behave identically on average so that zi+1,k¯z_{i+1,\overline{k}} describes any logit but the correct zi+1,kz_{i+1,k}. In this way, the loss can be expressed in terms of the order parameters together with an initialization-dependent constant. The mean-field loss describes both the single-seed loss and the seed-averaged loss very well; see Fig. 4 in the appendix.

For the correct next-token logit zi+1,kz_{i+1,k}, the teacher logit vector 𝐩𝐢+𝟏⋆\mathbf{p_{i+1}^{\star}} is one-hot, with unity at entry kk. It can be expressed using the exact teacher construction. The expectation value is taken over the local action and state. In principle, it can be reduced to an average over the actions and the initial state, since permutation composition preserves the relevant statistics. These variables are statistically independent, and a uniform distribution suffices to describe the random drawing of input tokens. In the ensemble, no step in the state sequence is preferred, so πi,i−L=A\pi_{i,i-L}=A describes the relevant attention entries well. This behavior can also be observed directly during training; for details, see Fig. 5 in the appendix. Ultimately, this yields the mean correct logit:

⟨zi+1,k⟩\displaystyle\langle z_{i+1,k}\rangle =(A+1−Adg)​R+dg−1dg​(1−A)​S.\displaystyle=\biggl(A+\frac{1-A}{d_{g}}\biggr)R+\frac{d_{g}-1}{d_{g}}\,(1-A)S\ . (11)

The dependence on the sequence position ii disappears after averaging.

The mean other logits can be obtained from the average total logit, independently of which state label is correct. Because the sum of the logits remains constant under cross-entropy training without weight decay, the correct logit is closely tied to the remaining ones. Explicitly, we find

⟨zi+1,k¯⟩\displaystyle\langle z_{i+1,\overline{k}}\rangle =−⟨zi+1,k⟩N−1+1dg​N​(N−1)​∑a=1dg∑r,s=1N[Ma]r​s,\displaystyle=-\frac{\langle z_{i+1,k}\rangle}{N-1}+\frac{1}{d_{g}N(N-1)}\sum_{a=1}^{d_{g}}\sum_{r,s=1}^{N}\bigl[M_{a}\bigr]_{rs}\ , (12)

where the sum of learnable matrices depends on the initialization and remains constant throughout training. We expect the mean correct logit to grow during training. When it does, the remaining logits decrease, so the network progressively suppresses all incorrect classes.

4.3 Training dynamics

Autoregressive training induces discrete updates of the microscopic network parameters in the negative gradient direction of the exact loss. Under the mean-field ansatz, the update for a representative learnable matrix entry is

[Ma]r​s↦[Ma]r​s+Δ​[Ma]r​s,Δ​[Ma]r​s=−η​d​ℓCEd​[Ma]r​s,\displaystyle[M_{a}]_{rs}\mapsto[M_{a}]_{rs}+\Delta[M_{a}]_{rs}\ ,\qquad\Delta[M_{a}]_{rs}=-\eta\,\frac{\mathrm{d}\ell_{\mathrm{CE}}}{\mathrm{d}[M_{a}]_{rs}}\ , (13)

where η\eta is the learning rate and ℓCE\ell_{\mathrm{CE}} is the mean-field loss as a function of all network parameters. We define the training time α\alpha by α:=# epochs/(dg​N)\alpha:=\text{\# epochs}/(d_{g}N). Then one epoch corresponds to Δ​α:=1/(dg​N)\Delta\alpha:=1/(d_{g}N), a small change in training time. The mean-field loss allows us to translate these microscopic updates into dynamics for the macroscopic order parameters. To that end, we assume that the attention mass on the correct action is exchangeable across sequence positions and described by AA. We average teacher-teacher matrix overlaps over seeds, and we close the attention-gradient factor as dg​N​[|∇𝐖𝐐A|2+|∇𝐖𝐊A|2]=L​cω​A​(1−A)d_{g}N[|\nabla_{\mathbf{W_{Q}}}A|^{2}+|\nabla_{\mathbf{W_{K}}}A|^{2}]=Lc_{\omega}A(1-A) with

cω\displaystyle c_{\omega} :=2​dg​NL⁡(L−1)σ2⋅2dh∑n=1dh/2[1−1L2(sin⁡(ωn​L/2)sin⁡(ωn/2))2]2\displaystyle:=\frac{2d_{g}N}{L(L-1)}\,\sigma^{2}\cdot\frac{2}{d_{h}}\sum_{n=1}^{d_{h}/2}\Biggl[1-\frac{1}{L^{2}}\biggl(\frac{\sin(\omega_{n}L/2)}{\sin(\omega_{n}/2)}\biggr)^{2}\Biggr]^{2} (14)

determined by the initialization. Here, σ2\sigma^{2} is the variance of the key/query initialization and {ωn}n=1dh/2\{\omega_{n}\}_{n=1}^{d_{h}/2} are the RoPE frequencies. In our case, the default PyTorch nn.Linear initialization gives σ2=1/3\sigma^{2}=\nicefrac{{1}}{{3}}. Consequently, Δ​A\Delta A, Δ​R\Delta R, and Δ​S\Delta S become functions of the order parameters themselves and the network hyperparameters. We then take the thermodynamic limit dg,N,L,dh→∞d_{g},N,L,d_{h}\to\infty while keeping dg/Nd_{g}/N, N/LN/L, and L/dhL/d_{h} finite. In this limit, Δ​α→0\Delta\alpha\to 0, which allows us to pass from difference quotients to continuous derivatives, e.g., from Δ​S/Δ​α\Delta S/\Delta\alpha to d​S/d​α\mathrm{d}S/\mathrm{d}\alpha. This step is justified when the difference quotient converges uniformly on compact time intervals [45], which can be ensured in the gradient-flow limit. Here, this is consistent with the finite-ratio assumptions on the hyperparameters. Under this mean-field closure, the macroscopic order parameters satisfy

d​Ad​α\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}A}{\mathrm{d}\alpha} =η​11+1N−1​em⁡(A,R,S)​NN−1​dg−1dg​cω⋅L​A​(1−A)​(R−S),\displaystyle=\eta\,\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{N-1}\,\mathrm{e}^{m(A,R,S)}}\frac{N}{N-1}\frac{d_{g}-1}{d_{g}}\,c_{\omega}\cdot LA(1-A)(R-S)\ , (15a)
d​Rd​α\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}R}{\mathrm{d}\alpha} =η​11+1N−1​em⁡(A,R,S)⋅(A+1−Adg),\displaystyle=\eta\,\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{N-1}\,\mathrm{e}^{m(A,R,S)}}\cdot\biggl(A+\frac{1-A}{d_{g}}\biggr)\ , (15b)
d​Sd​α\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}S}{\mathrm{d}\alpha} =η​11+1N−1​em⁡(A,R,S)⋅1−Adg,\displaystyle=\eta\,\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{N-1}\,\mathrm{e}^{m(A,R,S)}}\cdot\frac{1-A}{d_{g}}\ , (15c)

where m⁡(A,R,S)m(A,R,S) is the logit margin: m⁡(A,R,S)=1L​∑i=L+12​L(⟨zi+1,k⟩−⟨zi+1,k¯⟩)m(A,R,S)=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=L+1}^{2L}(\langle z_{i+1,k}\rangle-\langle z_{i+1,\overline{k}}\rangle), which can be expressed through Eqs. (11) and (12). In Fig. 2, we compare empirical results with numerical solutions of these differential equations. The initial conditions are A⁡(0)=1/LA(0)=1/L and R⁡(0)=S⁡(0)=0R(0)=S(0)=0. The agreement is very good. We see a clear transition in the attention mechanism: at short times α≲1\alpha\lesssim 1, AA remains near its initial value A⁡(0)A(0); later, it rises rapidly to saturation. In the same time regimes, RR first increases slowly and then quickly aligns with the teacher once the attention head has started learning. By contrast, the overlap with the non-matching teacher matrices, SS, increases relatively quickly at first and saturates once attention is nearly perfect.

Interpretation

During early training, the model learns a heuristic in the logic module: the student matrices acquire mixed directions. The attention output weights the actions in the sequence nearly uniformly, so the logic module cannot yet apply the correct action to the current state. Instead, the next state is predicted by applying a mixture of actions, and both the correct overlaps RR and the off-target overlaps SS increase. This changes once attention begins to distinguish the correct action from the others. At that point, the learnable matrices begin to align strongly with the teacher matrices, which in turn reinforces correct action selection in the attention block. This MLP-first regime is consistent with gradient-flow analyses of transformer training, in which task-relevant linear or MLP directions emerge before attention has appreciably specialized [29]. The resulting transition resembles later-stage attention specialization, although here it is tied specifically to selecting the correct state-update rule rather than to co-occurrence recognition or induction-head formation [30, 31].

5 Final rollout accuracy

Ultimately, the model should correctly predict the final token in the sequence, once the intermediate steps are learned well enough; that is, it should carry out a chain of thought without making errors along the way. In this section, we model the accuracy of the final token. At each step in the sequence, the model may predict either the correct next state or an incorrect one. Accordingly, the probability of a correct prediction obeys the recursion

P⁡(s^t+1=st+1)\displaystyle P(\hat{s}_{t+1}=s_{t+1}) =P⁡(s^t=st)⋅P⁡(s^t+1=st+1|s^t=st)\displaystyle=P(\hat{s}_{t}=s_{t})\cdot P(\hat{s}_{t+1}=s_{t+1}|\hat{s}_{t}=s_{t})
+[1−P(s^t=st)]⋅P(s^t+1=st+1|s^t≠st).\displaystyle\quad+\bigl[1-P(\hat{s}_{t}=s_{t})\bigr]\cdot P(\hat{s}_{t+1}=s_{t+1}|\hat{s}_{t}\neq s_{t})\ . (16)

Since the initial token is given, we have P⁡(s^0=s0)=1P(\hat{s}_{0}=s_{0})=1. In principle, the model can recover the correct token even when acting on an incorrect current state, although this effect becomes less important as training progresses.

Both conditional probabilities in Eq. (16) depend on the logit distributions. Empirically, the logits are approximately normally distributed at initialization and during the early stages of training. Assuming that the correct logit follows a Gaussian distribution 𝒩⁡(μk,σk2)\mathcal{N}(\mu_{k},\sigma^{2}_{k}) and that each incorrect logit follows 𝒩⁡(μk¯,σk¯2)\mathcal{N}(\mu_{\overline{k}},\sigma^{2}_{\overline{k}}), we can model these conditional probabilities. For the next-token accuracy, we obtain P⁡(s^t+1=st+1|s^t=st)=ρP(\hat{s}_{t+1}=s_{t+1}|\hat{s}_{t}=s_{t})=\rho for any t∈{0,…,L−1}t\in\{0,\dotsc,L-1\}, with

ρ\displaystyle\rho =∫−∞+∞d​u​e−u2/22​π​Φ​(σkσk¯​u+μk−μk¯σk¯)N−1.\displaystyle=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\mathrm{d}u\,\frac{\mathrm{e}^{-u^{2}/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,\Phi\!\biggl(\frac{\sigma_{k}}{\sigma_{\overline{k}}}\,u+\frac{\mu_{k}-\mu_{\overline{k}}}{\sigma_{\overline{k}}}\biggr)^{N-1}\ . (17)

Furthermore, if the incorrect logits are symmetric and have no preference among themselves, the recovery term P⁡(s^t+1=st+1∣s^t≠st)P(\hat{s}_{t+1}=s_{t+1}\mid\hat{s}_{t}\neq s_{t}) can be written as (1−ρ)/(N−1)(1-\rho)/(N-1). Under this approximation, the final rollout accuracy becomes

P⁡(s^L=sL)\displaystyle P(\hat{s}_{L}=s_{L}) ≈N−1N​(N​ρ−1N−1)L+1N.\displaystyle\approx\frac{N-1}{N}\biggl(\frac{N\rho-1}{N-1}\biggr)^{L}+\frac{1}{N}\ . (18)

This expression is approximate for two reasons. First, training introduces correlations between the correct and incorrect logits, whereas the derivation assumes independence. Second, the logit distributions deviate from the Gaussian approximation as training proceeds. Even so, the formula captures the qualitative form of the transition even for constant variances σk2,σk¯2\sigma^{2}_{k},\sigma^{2}_{\overline{k}}; see Fig. 3. The rollout accuracy remains near its initial plateau of 1/N1/N, then rises sharply and saturates at unity. The reason for this sharp transition is clear from Eq. (18): the next-token accuracy enters to the LLth power, so even a gradual increase in one-step accuracy is converted into a sudden jump in the final rollout accuracy.

6 Discussion

Summary

This work studies a simplified transformer model for a compositional permutation task from a statistical-physics viewpoint. We introduce macroscopic order parameters to describe the learning dynamics of the attention head and the logic module (a specialized MLP). We find that the model first learns a heuristic, before the attention mechanism aligns with the teacher and effective learning takes place. We also derive a description of the accuracy of the final token in the chain of states: a justified approximation reproduces the empirically observed sudden increase qualitatively and shows that this emergent phenomenon, as a function of training time, arises from the compositional structure of the task. Taken together, these results shed light on the roles of the core components of a transformer in a controlled state-tracking problem.

Limitations

The architecture studied here is deliberately constrained and therefore does not represent a standard one-block transformer, let alone a full-scale transformer. Even so, it is plausible that similar learning phases may also occur in less specialized architectures on related tasks. Our analytical results rely on a mean-field description of the loss, which introduces approximations relative to the exact training dynamics. These approximations may behave differently in other models or on other tasks. More work is needed to determine how far the present picture extends to standard transformer architectures, how robust the staged learning dynamics are, and how they are affected by reinforcement learning after pretraining.

Appendix A Hyperparameters

Table 1 lists all hyperparameters used for the chief simulations. The RoPE frequencies are power-law distributed and set as ωn:=2πθRoPE−2(n−1)/dh\omega_{n}:=2\pi\,\theta_{\mathrm{RoPE}}^{-2(n-1)/d_{h}} with θRoPE\theta_{\mathrm{RoPE}} (rope_theta) as the base and n=1,…,dh/2n=1,\dots,d_{h}/2.

Appendix B Architecture Setup

For the model training, we use PyTorch. For the sake of reproducibility, we sketch the numeric setup as follows:

  • •

    Set seed with numpy.

  • •

    Set RoPE frequencies.

  • •

    Draw permutation vocabulary (dgd_{g}) using rng.permutation(N) with the default numpy random number generator of the seed, then create the permutation matrices.

  • •

    Generate dataset (sequences):

    • –

      Draw LL actions from the permutations and one initial index in [N][N].

    • –

      Build the teacher token sequence by sequential application of the permutations on the current state.

  • •

    Define class with pytorch using nn.Module.

  • •

    Initialize two linear layers (keys and queries) and a parameter tensor for the learnable matrices uniformly.

  • •

    Forward function:

    • –

      Embed the token, compute key and query, apply RoPE.

    • –

      Compute attention matrix (causal and restricted to actions).

    • –

      Compute attention output with Values.

    • –

      Compute logic module output with learnable matrices and current token.

  • •

    Train the model:

    • –

      Use train and test data loader for the dataset.

    • –

      Set optimizer (here SGD with batch size equal to train set size)

    • –

      For each epoch, predict the tokens, compute the loss, apply the optimizer, backwards propagation, and optimizer step.

    • –

      Evaluate every few epochs the train/test accuracies, the order parameters, and other computable quantities.

LLMs were used to write the code for training and analysis. It was subject to scrutiny before execution, and the code performs the intended purposes. The code is available in the supplementary material. To train the model, execute the Python script with command arguments --seed <int> --dir "str" for one seed, the output is saved as a numpy file in the given directory. The hyperparameters are set within the script’s code. To inspect the data, compute the theoretical predictions, and generate the figures displayed in this work, use the Python Notebook.

For training, several GPUs and a cluster were used. A T4 GPU takes 30 minutes to train one model (one seed), an NVIDIA Geforce RTX 4060 around 20 minutes. We used seeds 00 to 9999.

Many hyperparameter combinations were tested, hence more computational time was occupied than strictly necessary for the results shown here. The model learns robustly for changes in the hyperparameters N,dg,L,dhN,d_{g},L,d_{h} as well as the learning rate, RoPE frequency base and number of training examples.

Variations in dg,Nd_{g},N (between 88 and 3232) or LL (between 55 and 2020) or dhd_{h} (between 88 and 128128) also produce fully learned models. Fewer frequencies (dhd_{h}) limit the learnability. Linearly distributed frequencies yield a similar learning behavior as the power-law distributed ones used here. Appendix J shows figures for another set of hyperparameters than used in the main text.

Appendix C Realizing the logic module as a constrained MLP

The logic module used in the main text differs from the feed-forward block of a standard transformer because the module output is written directly as a weighted sum of learnable matrices. Nevertheless, this computation can be implemented by a GLU-style MLP once the MLP input is arranged so that the first dgd_{g} coordinates contain the action information 𝐨∈ℝdg\mathbf{o}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{g}} coming from attention and the last NN coordinates contain the current state 𝐬∈ℝN\mathbf{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}. The state vector is one-hot, whereas 𝐨\mathbf{o} may contain soft attention outputs.

Ignoring sequence indices, the desired logic computation is

𝐳\displaystyle\mathbf{z} :=∑a=1dgoa​Ma​𝐬=(M1,…,Mdg)​(o1​𝐬odg​𝐬),\displaystyle:=\sum_{a=1}^{d_{g}}o_{a}M_{a}\mathbf{s}=\bigl(M_{1},\dots,M_{d_{g}}\bigr)\begin{pmatrix}o_{1}\mathbf{s}\\ \vdots\\ o_{d_{g}}\mathbf{s}\end{pmatrix}\ , (19)

where Ma∈ℝN×NM_{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}, a=1,…,dga=1,\dots,d_{g}, are the learnable action matrices. We now show that the vector in the second factor can be produced by fixed up- and gate-projections.

Consider a GLU-style MLP without biases,

𝐳MLP\displaystyle\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{MLP}} :=Wd​[Wu​(𝐨𝐬)⊙ϕ⁡(Wg​(𝐨𝐬))].\displaystyle:=W_{d}\left[W_{u}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{o}\\ \mathbf{s}\end{pmatrix}\odot\phi\!\left(W_{g}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{o}\\ \mathbf{s}\end{pmatrix}\right)\right]\ . (20)

We take the activation to be the identity, ϕ⁡(x)=x\phi(x)=x. The up-projection is fixed to copy the state vector into dgd_{g} blocks,

Wu:=(0N×dgIN0N×dgIN)∈ℝdg​N×(dg+N),Wu​(𝐨𝐬)=(𝐬𝐬).\displaystyle W_{u}:=\begin{pmatrix}0_{N\times d_{g}}&I_{N}\\ \vdots&\vdots\\ 0_{N\times d_{g}}&I_{N}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{g}N\times(d_{g}+N)}\ ,\qquad W_{u}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{o}\\ \mathbf{s}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{s}\\ \vdots\\ \mathbf{s}\end{pmatrix}\ . (21)

The gate projection is fixed to copy each action coordinate over one state-sized block. Let Ta∈ℝN×dgT_{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{g}} denote the matrix whose aa-th column is all ones and whose other entries are zero. Let 𝟏𝐍∈ℝN\mathbf{1_{N}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} denote the all-ones vector. Set

Wg:=(T10N×NTdg0N×N)∈ℝdg​N×(dg+N),Wg​(𝐨𝐬)=(o1​𝟏Nodg​𝟏N).\displaystyle W_{g}:=\begin{pmatrix}T_{1}&0_{N\times N}\\ \vdots&\vdots\\ T_{d_{g}}&0_{N\times N}\end{pmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{g}N\times(d_{g}+N)}\ ,\qquad W_{g}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{o}\\ \mathbf{s}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}o_{1}\mathbf{1}_{N}\\ \vdots\\ o_{d_{g}}\mathbf{1}_{N}\end{pmatrix}. (22)

Therefore, multiplying the two projections of Eqs. (21) and (22) element wise gives the rightmost vector of Eq. (19). Finally, choose the down-projection as Wd:=(M1,…,Mdg)∈ℝN×dg​NW_{d}:=\bigl(M_{1},\dots,M_{d_{g}}\bigr)\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{g}N}. With this choice, Eqs. (19)–(22) imply 𝐳MLP=𝐳\mathbf{z}_{\mathrm{MLP}}=\mathbf{z} for the linear activation ϕ⁡(x)=x\phi(x)=x. Thus, the specialized logic module is representable as a GLU-style MLP with fixed up-projection and gate-projection weights and learnable down-projection blocks.

Embeddings

Similarly to the logic module, the attention head can be implemented from a default attention architecture. With the bundled embedding structure introduced above, i.e., a (dg+N)(d_{g}+N)-dimensional embedding with one-hot vectors for the actions and states, we define key and query matrices WK,WQ∈ℝdh×(dg+N)W_{K},W_{Q}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}\times(d_{g}+N)} as

WK=((WK)1⋯(WK)1(WK)dh⋯(WK)dh),WQ=((WQ)1⋯(WQ)1(WQ)dh⋯(WQ)dh).\displaystyle W_{K}=\begin{pmatrix}(W_{K})_{1}&\cdots&(W_{K})_{1}\\ \vdots&&\vdots\\ (W_{K})_{d_{h}}&\cdots&(W_{K})_{d_{h}}\end{pmatrix}\ ,\quad W_{Q}=\begin{pmatrix}(W_{Q})_{1}&\cdots&(W_{Q})_{1}\\ \vdots&&\vdots\\ (W_{Q})_{d_{h}}&\cdots&(W_{Q})_{d_{h}}\end{pmatrix}\ . (23)

The first column is repeated dg+Nd_{g}+N times. In that regard, the weight matrix reduces to one learnable vector. Then, any embedded vector 𝐮𝐢∈ℝdg+N\mathbf{u_{i}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{g}+N} is one-hot, because it is either an action or a state. This yields

WK​(𝐠𝟎N)=((WQ)1(WQ)dh),WK​(𝟎dg𝐬)=((WQ)1(WQ)dh),\displaystyle W_{K}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{g}\\ \mathbf{0}_{N}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}(W_{Q})_{1}\\ \vdots\\ (W_{Q})_{d_{h}}\end{pmatrix}\ ,\qquad W_{K}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{0}_{d_{g}}\\ \mathbf{s}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}(W_{Q})_{1}\\ \vdots\\ (W_{Q})_{d_{h}}\end{pmatrix}\ , (24)

and equally for WQW_{Q}, for any one-hot encoded action 𝐠\mathbf{g} or state 𝐬\mathbf{s}. This is completely equivalent to choosing a unit embedding and key/query vectors such that 𝐖𝐊​𝐮𝐢=𝐖𝐊\mathbf{W_{K}}\mathbf{u_{i}}=\mathbf{W_{K}} with 𝐮𝐢=1∈ℝ1\mathbf{u_{i}}=1\in\mathbb{R}^{1}. Consequently, we may write the keys and queries as vectors and omit the embedding in the attention head.

Appendix D Derivation of the mean correct/other logits

D.1 Mean correct logit

The next correct logit zi+1,kz_{i+1,k} following position ii in the LL-sequence can be computed directly. Predictions are made only for the states following positions i=L+1,…,2​Li=L+1,\dotsc,2L; and for these prediction positions, we have

zi+1,k=𝐩𝐢+𝟏⋆⋅𝐳𝐢+𝟏\displaystyle z_{i+1,k}=\mathbf{p_{i+1}^{\star}}\cdot\mathbf{z_{i+1}} (25)

where 𝐩𝐢+𝟏⋆\mathbf{p_{i+1}^{\star}} is the teacher “logit” vector, a one-hot vector with unity at entry kk. This gives

zi+1,k\displaystyle z_{i+1,k} =∑a,b=1dg𝐞𝐱𝐢⊤​(Ma⋆)⊤​Mb​𝐞𝐱𝐢​(∑j≤iπi​j​(vj)b)​(vi−L)a\displaystyle=\sum_{a,b=1}^{d_{g}}\mathbf{e_{x_{i}}^{\top}}(M_{a}^{\star})^{\top}M_{b}\mathbf{e_{x_{i}}}\left(\sum_{j\leq i}\pi_{ij}(v_{j})_{b}\right)(v_{i-L})_{a} (26)

Here, 𝐞𝐱𝐢∈ℝN\mathbf{e_{x_{i}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} is a state token written as a one-hot encoded (OHE) vector. Similarly, the value vector 𝐯j\mathbf{v}_{j} from the transformer is an OHE vector for the actions, but zero for the states:

𝐯j:={𝐞^𝐠𝐣,j=1,…,L𝟎,j≥L+1\displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{j}:=\begin{cases}\mathbf{\hat{e}_{g_{j}}}\ ,\quad&j=1,\dotsc,L\\ \mathbf{0}\ ,\quad&j\geq L+1\end{cases} (27)

with unit vectors in ℝdg\mathbb{R}^{d_{g}}. Each gjg_{j}, j=1,…,Lj=1,\dotsc,L, specifies the action among the dgd_{g} permutations in the vocabulary.

We combine the facts that i≥L+1i\geq L+1 here and that 𝐯j\mathbf{v}_{j} is identically zero for j≥L+1j\geq L+1 to rewrite the inner sum:

zi+1,k\displaystyle z_{i+1,k} =∑a,b=1dg[(Ma⋆)⊤​Mb]xi​xi​(∑j=1Lπi​j​δgj,b​δgi−L,a)\displaystyle=\sum_{a,b=1}^{d_{g}}\Bigl[(M_{a}^{\star})^{\top}M_{b}\Bigr]_{x_{i}x_{i}}\biggl(\sum_{j=1}^{L}\pi_{ij}\delta_{g_{j},b}\delta_{g_{i-L},a}\biggr) (28)
=∑a,b=1dg[(Ma⋆)⊤​Mb]xi​xi​(πi,i−L​δgi−L,b​δgi−L,a+∑j=1j≠i−LLπi​j​δgj,b​δgi−L,a)\displaystyle=\sum_{a,b=1}^{d_{g}}\Bigl[(M_{a}^{\star})^{\top}M_{b}\Bigr]_{x_{i}x_{i}}\biggl(\pi_{i,i-L}\delta_{g_{i-L},b}\delta_{g_{i-L},a}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j=1\\ j\neq i-L\end{subarray}}^{L}\pi_{ij}\delta_{g_{j},b}\delta_{g_{i-L},a}\biggr) (29)

One model trains on a large number of training examples. To account for the average behavior, we have to take an expectation value w.r.t. the current state xix_{i} and all the actions gjg_{j}, j∈{1,…,L}j\in\{1,\dotsc,L\}. Here, all actions are needed, because the attention output depends on all those actions via the Values. Because the current state can be obtained by the chain of permutations, the average w.r.t. xi=si−L−1x_{i}=s_{i-L-1} is equivalent to an average over the initial state s0s_{0}, when simultaneously averaging over the actions. We assume a uniform probability distribution for all quantities. These two averages are then statistically independent.

We apply the expectation value and rewrite δgi−L,b​δgi−L,a=δa​b​δgi−L,a\delta_{g_{i-L},b}\delta_{g_{i-L},a}=\delta_{ab}\delta_{g_{i-L},a}:

⟨zi+1,k⟩\displaystyle\langle z_{i+1,k}\rangle =1N∑xi=1N1dgL∑g1=1dg∑g2=1dg…∑gL=1dg\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{x_{i}=1}^{N}\frac{1}{d_{g}^{L}}\sum_{g_{1}=1}^{d_{g}}\sum_{g_{2}=1}^{d_{g}}\dotsc\sum_{g_{L}=1}^{d_{g}} (30)
×(∑a,b=1dg[(Ma⋆)⊤​Mb]xi​xi​(πi,i−L​δa​b​δgi−L,a+∑j=1j≠i−LLπi​j​δgj,b​δgi−L,a))\displaystyle\quad\times\Biggl(\sum_{a,b=1}^{d_{g}}\Bigl[(M_{a}^{\star})^{\top}M_{b}\Bigr]_{x_{i}x_{i}}\biggl(\pi_{i,i-L}\delta_{ab}\delta_{g_{i-L},a}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j=1\\ j\neq i-L\end{subarray}}^{L}\pi_{ij}\delta_{g_{j},b}\delta_{g_{i-L},a}\biggr)\Biggr) (31)

Then, we get

⟨zi+1,k⟩\displaystyle\langle z_{i+1,k}\rangle =∑a,b=1dg1N​Tr⁡[(Ma⋆)⊤​Mb]​(πi,i−L​δa​bdg+∑j=1j≠i−LLπi​j​1dg2)\displaystyle=\sum_{a,b=1}^{d_{g}}\frac{1}{N}\Tr\Bigl[(M_{a}^{\star})^{\top}M_{b}\Bigr]\biggl(\pi_{i,i-L}\,\frac{\delta_{ab}}{d_{g}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j=1\\ j\neq i-L\end{subarray}}^{L}\pi_{ij}\frac{1}{d_{g}^{2}}\biggr) (32)
=∑a,b=1dg1N​Tr⁡[(Ma⋆)⊤​Mb]​[πi,i−L​(δa​bdg−1dg2)+1dg2]\displaystyle=\sum_{a,b=1}^{d_{g}}\frac{1}{N}\Tr\Bigl[(M_{a}^{\star})^{\top}M_{b}\Bigr]\biggl[\pi_{i,i-L}\biggl(\frac{\delta_{ab}}{d_{g}}-\frac{1}{d_{g}^{2}}\biggr)+\frac{1}{d_{g}^{2}}\biggr] (33)
=πi,i−L​R+(1−πi,i−L)​1dg2​∑a,b=1dg1N​Tr⁡[(Ma⋆)⊤​Mb]\displaystyle=\pi_{i,i-L}R+(1-\pi_{i,i-L})\frac{1}{d_{g}^{2}}\sum_{a,b=1}^{d_{g}}\frac{1}{N}\Tr\Bigl[(M_{a}^{\star})^{\top}M_{b}\Bigr] (34)
=(πi,i−L+1−πi,i−Ldg)​R+dg−1dg​(1−πi,i−L)​S\displaystyle=\biggl(\pi_{i,i-L}+\frac{1-\pi_{i,i-L}}{d_{g}}\biggr)R+\frac{d_{g}-1}{d_{g}}(1-\pi_{i,i-L})S (35)

Let us assume that there is no preferred step in the sequence; then we can use the ansatz πi+L,i=A\pi_{i+L,i}=A. This is empirically confirmed by the attention entries’s evolution during training shown in Fig. 5. Consequently,

⟨zi+1,k⟩\displaystyle\langle z_{i+1,k}\rangle =(A+1−Adg)​R+dg−1dg​(1−A)​S\displaystyle=\biggl(A+\frac{1-A}{d_{g}}\biggr)R+\frac{d_{g}-1}{d_{g}}(1-A)S (36)

D.2 Mean other logits

Starting with the expression for the logit vector, we calculate the average logit first. For any r=1,…,Nr=1,\dotsc,N, we have

zi+1,r\displaystyle z_{i+1,r} =𝐳i+1⋅𝐞r=∑a=1dg𝐞r⊤​Ma​𝐞xi​∑j=1Lπi​j​(vj)a=∑a=1dg[Ma]r​xi​∑j=1Lπi​j​δgj​a\displaystyle=\mathbf{z}_{i+1}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{r}=\sum_{a=1}^{d_{g}}\mathbf{e}_{r}^{\top}M_{a}\mathbf{e}_{x_{i}}\sum_{j=1}^{L}\pi_{ij}(v_{j})_{a}=\sum_{a=1}^{d_{g}}\bigl[M_{a}\bigr]_{rx_{i}}\sum_{j=1}^{L}\pi_{ij}\delta_{g_{j}a} (37)

and in the expectation value,

⟨zi+1,r⟩\displaystyle\langle z_{i+1,r}\rangle =1N​∑xi=1N1dgL​∑g1=1dg∑g2=1dg…​∑gL=1dg∑a=1dg[Ma]r​xi​∑j=1Lπi​j​δgj​a\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{x_{i}=1}^{N}\frac{1}{d_{g}^{L}}\sum_{g_{1}=1}^{d_{g}}\sum_{g_{2}=1}^{d_{g}}\dotsc\sum_{g_{L}=1}^{d_{g}}\sum_{a=1}^{d_{g}}\bigl[M_{a}\bigr]_{rx_{i}}\sum_{j=1}^{L}\pi_{ij}\delta_{g_{j}a} (38)
=1dg​N​∑s=1N∑a=1dg[Ma]r​s​∑j=1Lπi​j\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d_{g}N}\sum_{s=1}^{N}\sum_{a=1}^{d_{g}}\bigl[M_{a}\bigr]_{rs}\sum_{j=1}^{L}\pi_{ij} (39)

The sum over the attention rows are exactly 1 for all i≥L+1i\geq L+1 with our construction. The sum of all logits remains constant throughout the training due to the combination of cross-entropy loss and gradient flow. Hence, we define the constant parameter ζinit\zeta_{\mathrm{init}} as the sum of the logits:

ζinit\displaystyle\zeta_{\mathrm{init}} :=1dg​N​∑a=1dg∑r,s=1N[Ma]r​s\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{d_{g}N}\sum_{a=1}^{d_{g}}\sum_{r,s=1}^{N}\bigl[M_{a}\bigr]_{rs} (40)

Now, we obtained the average expression for any logit. That is, for some initializations, rr is the correct logit’s index; for many others, rr is the index for some other logit. As we are interested in the definite, non-correct logit here and already have an identity for the mean correct logit, we define

⟨zi+1,k¯⟩:=1N−1​(ζinit−⟨zi+1,k⟩)\displaystyle\langle z_{i+1,\overline{k}}\rangle:=\frac{1}{N-1}\Bigl(\zeta_{\mathrm{init}}-\langle z_{i+1,k}\rangle\Bigr) (41)

As ζinit\zeta_{\mathrm{init}} is fundamentally a quantity depending on the model initialization, different seeds will yield different dynamics of the mean other logits and thus of the order parameters.

Appendix E Differential equations for the order parameters

The micro-parameter change, obtained from the discrete learning update step, is described by

Δ​[Ma]r​s​(α):=[Ma]r​s​(α+Δ​α)−[Ma]r​s​(α)=−η​d​ℓCEd​[Ma]r​s\displaystyle\Delta[M_{a}]_{rs}(\alpha):=[M_{a}]_{rs}(\alpha+\Delta\alpha)-[M_{a}]_{rs}(\alpha)=-\eta\,\frac{\mathrm{d}\ell_{\mathrm{CE}}}{\mathrm{d}[M_{a}]_{rs}} (42)

We write the derivative w.r.t. the micro-parameters via the mean correct/other logits with the chain rule. For them, we find the relation

∂ℓCE∂⟨zi+1,k⟩=−∂ℓCE∂⟨zi+1,k¯⟩\displaystyle\frac{\partial\ell_{\mathrm{CE}}}{\partial\langle z_{i+1,k}\rangle}=-\frac{\partial\ell_{\mathrm{CE}}}{\partial\langle z_{i+1,\overline{k}}\rangle} (43)

Mean correct/other logit derivatives

Using the expression for the mean correct logit (11), it is

d​⟨zi+1,k⟩d​[Mb]r​s\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}\langle z_{i+1,k}\rangle}{\mathrm{d}[M_{b}]_{rs}} =∂⟨zi+1,k⟩∂R​d​Rd​[Mb]r​s+∂⟨zi+1,k⟩∂S​d​Sd​[Mb]r​s\displaystyle=\frac{\partial\langle z_{i+1,k}\rangle}{\partial R}\frac{\mathrm{d}R}{\mathrm{d}[M_{b}]_{rs}}+\frac{\partial\langle z_{i+1,k}\rangle}{\partial S}\frac{\mathrm{d}S}{\mathrm{d}[M_{b}]_{rs}} (44)
=cR​d​Rd​[Mb]r​s+cS​d​Sd​[Mb]r​s\displaystyle=c_{R}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}R}{\mathrm{d}[M_{b}]_{rs}}+c_{S}\,\frac{\mathrm{d}S}{\mathrm{d}[M_{b}]_{rs}} (45)

There is no derivative of AA here, because AA does not depend on the learned permutation matrices at all. The parameters cR,cSc_{R},c_{S} are given by

cR:=A+1−Adg,cS=dg−1dg​(1−A)=1−cR\displaystyle c_{R}:=A+\frac{1-A}{d_{g}}\ ,\quad c_{S}=\frac{d_{g}-1}{d_{g}}(1-A)=1-c_{R} (46)

One can show that

d​Rd​[Mb]r​s\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}R}{\mathrm{d}[M_{b}]_{rs}} =1dg​N​[Mb⋆]r​s,d​Sd​[Mb]r​s=1dg​(dg−1)​N​∑c=1c≠bdg[Mc⋆]r​s\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d_{g}N}\,[M^{\star}_{b}]_{rs}\ ,\qquad\frac{\mathrm{d}S}{\mathrm{d}[M_{b}]_{rs}}=\frac{1}{d_{g}(d_{g}-1)N}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c=1\\ c\neq b\end{subarray}}^{d_{g}}[M^{\star}_{c}]_{rs} (47)

Thus,

d​⟨zi+1,k⟩d​[Mb]r​s\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}\langle z_{i+1,k}\rangle}{\mathrm{d}[M_{b}]_{rs}} =cRdg​N​[Mb⋆]r​s+cSdg​(dg−1)​N​∑c=1c≠bdg[Mc⋆]r​s\displaystyle=\frac{c_{R}}{d_{g}N}\,[M^{\star}_{b}]_{rs}+\frac{c_{S}}{d_{g}(d_{g}-1)N}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c=1\\ c\neq b\end{subarray}}^{d_{g}}[M^{\star}_{c}]_{rs} (48)

Take the expression for the mean other logit (41), then

d​⟨zi+1,k¯⟩d​[Mb]r​s\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}\langle z_{i+1,\overline{k}}\rangle}{\mathrm{d}[M_{b}]_{rs}} =−1N−1​d​⟨zi+1,k⟩d​[Mb]r​s+1N−1​1dg​N\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{N-1}\frac{\mathrm{d}\langle z_{i+1,k}\rangle}{\mathrm{d}[M_{b}]_{rs}}+\frac{1}{N-1}\frac{1}{d_{g}N} (49)

Before we resolve this expression, it is best to advance to the update for [Mb]r​s[M_{b}]_{rs}.

The micro-parameter update.

Due to the opposing minus signs in the mean correct/other logits in the loss expression, we get a simplification in

Δ​[Mb]r​s\displaystyle\Delta[M_{b}]_{rs} =−η⁡(∂ℓCE∂⟨zi+1,k⟩​d​⟨zi+1,k⟩d​[Mb]r​s+∂ℓCE∂⟨zi+1,k¯⟩​d​⟨zi+1,k¯⟩d​[Mb]r​s)\displaystyle=-\eta\biggl(\frac{\partial\ell_{\mathrm{CE}}}{\partial\langle z_{i+1,k}\rangle}\frac{\mathrm{d}\langle z_{i+1,k}\rangle}{\mathrm{d}[M_{b}]_{rs}}+\frac{\partial\ell_{\mathrm{CE}}}{\partial\langle z_{i+1,\overline{k}}\rangle}\frac{\mathrm{d}\langle z_{i+1,\overline{k}}\rangle}{\mathrm{d}[M_{b}]_{rs}}\biggr) (50)
=−η​∂ℓCE∂⟨zi+1,k⟩​NN−1​(d​⟨zi+1,k⟩d​[Mb]r​s−1dg​N2)\displaystyle=-\eta\,\frac{\partial\ell_{\mathrm{CE}}}{\partial\langle z_{i+1,k}\rangle}\frac{N}{N-1}\biggl(\frac{\mathrm{d}\langle z_{i+1,k}\rangle}{\mathrm{d}[M_{b}]_{rs}}-\frac{1}{d_{g}N^{2}}\biggr) (51)

and we can now plug in the mean correct logit derivative:

Δ​[Mb]r​s\displaystyle\Delta[M_{b}]_{rs} =−ηdg​N​∂ℓCE∂⟨zi+1,k⟩​NN−1​[cR​[Mb⋆]r​s+cSdg−1​∑c=1c≠bdg[Mc⋆]r​s−1N]\displaystyle=-\frac{\eta}{d_{g}N}\frac{\partial\ell_{\mathrm{CE}}}{\partial\langle z_{i+1,k}\rangle}\frac{N}{N-1}\Biggl[c_{R}\,[M^{\star}_{b}]_{rs}+\frac{c_{S}}{d_{g}-1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c=1\\ c\neq b\end{subarray}}^{d_{g}}[M^{\star}_{c}]_{rs}-\frac{1}{N}\Biggr] (52)

Order parameter updates

With the order parameter definitions of RR and SS, we find

Δ​R\displaystyle\Delta R =1dg​∑a=1dg1N​Tr⁡[(Ma⋆)⊤​Δ​Ma]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d_{g}}\sum_{a=1}^{d_{g}}\frac{1}{N}\Tr\Bigl[(M^{\star}_{a})^{\top}\Delta M_{a}\Bigr] (53)
=−ηdg​N​∂ℓCE∂⟨zi+1,k⟩​NN−1​(cR+cS​τ−1N)\displaystyle=-\frac{\eta}{d_{g}N}\,\frac{\partial\ell_{\mathrm{CE}}}{\partial\langle z_{i+1,k}\rangle}\frac{N}{N-1}\biggl(c_{R}+c_{S}\tau-\frac{1}{N}\biggr) (54)

because the teacher matrices are fixed for one seed, and

Δ​S\displaystyle\Delta S =1dg​(dg−1)​∑a=1dg∑b=1b≠adg1N​Tr⁡[(Ma⋆)⊤​Δ​Mb]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d_{g}(d_{g}-1)}\sum_{a=1}^{d_{g}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b=1\\ b\neq a\end{subarray}}^{d_{g}}\frac{1}{N}\Tr\Bigl[(M^{\star}_{a})^{\top}\Delta M_{b}\Bigr] (55)
=−ηdg​N​∂ℓCE∂⟨zi+1,k⟩​NN−1​(cR​τ+cS​dg−2dg−1​σ+cSdg−1−1N)\displaystyle=-\frac{\eta}{d_{g}N}\,\frac{\partial\ell_{\mathrm{CE}}}{\partial\langle z_{i+1,k}\rangle}\frac{N}{N-1}\biggl(c_{R}\tau+c_{S}\,\frac{d_{g}-2}{d_{g}-1}\,\sigma+\frac{c_{S}}{d_{g}-1}-\frac{1}{N}\biggr) (56)

Two constants appear, τ\tau and σ\sigma. They are defined as

τ\displaystyle\tau :=1dg​(dg−1)​N​∑a=1dg∑c=1c≠adgTr⁡[(Ma⋆)⊤​Mc⋆]\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{d_{g}(d_{g}-1)N}\sum_{a=1}^{d_{g}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c=1\\ c\neq a\end{subarray}}^{d_{g}}\Tr\Bigl[\bigl(M^{\star}_{a}\bigr)^{\top}M^{\star}_{c}\Bigr] (57)

and

σ\displaystyle\sigma :=1dg​(dg−1)​(dg−2)​N​∑a=1dg∑b=1b≠adg∑c=1c≠a,bdgTr⁡[(Ma⋆)⊤​Mc⋆]\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{d_{g}(d_{g}-1)(d_{g}-2)N}\sum_{a=1}^{d_{g}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b=1\\ b\neq a\end{subarray}}^{d_{g}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}c=1\\ c\neq a,b\end{subarray}}^{d_{g}}\Tr\Bigl[\bigl(M^{\star}_{a}\bigr)^{\top}M^{\star}_{c}\Bigr] (58)

and depend on the seed. We readily find σ=τ\sigma=\tau and are left with one such permutation matrix trace. As permutation matrices are not orthogonal, there is some overlap.

Many seeds give rise to many choices for the set of permutations. We can average over the seeds to get τ¯=1/N+ε\overline{\tau}=1/N+\varepsilon with a correction ε=−(1−1/N)/(N!−1)\varepsilon=-(1-1/N)/(N!-1), which is negligible for non-small NN. Details on this average are given in Appendix F. The final difference quotients using our mean-field cross-entropy then read

Δ​R\displaystyle\Delta R =ηdg​N​11+1N−1​em⁡(A,R,S)​(A+1−Adg)\displaystyle=\frac{\eta}{d_{g}N}\,\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{N-1}\,\mathrm{e}^{m(A,R,S)}}\biggl(A+\frac{1-A}{d_{g}}\biggr) (59a)
Δ​S\displaystyle\Delta S =ηdg​N​11+1N−1​em⁡(A,R,S)​1−Adg\displaystyle=\frac{\eta}{d_{g}N}\,\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{N-1}\,\mathrm{e}^{m(A,R,S)}}\frac{1-A}{d_{g}} (59b)

with m⁡(A,R,S)=1L​∑i=L+12​L⟨zi+1,k⟩−⟨zi+1,k¯⟩m(A,R,S)=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=L+1}^{2L}\langle z_{i+1,k}\rangle-\langle z_{i+1,\overline{k}}\rangle

The attention order parameter

To see the dynamics of AA, we write, for the moment, 𝐖=(𝐖𝐊⊤,𝐖𝐐⊤)⊤\mathbf{W}=(\mathbf{W_{K}^{\top}},\mathbf{W_{Q}^{\top}})^{\top} as a vector of all key and query weights. We calculate

dg​N​(∇𝐖A)⋅(−η)​(∇𝐖ℓCE)\displaystyle d_{g}N(\nabla_{\mathbf{W}}A)\cdot(-\eta)(\nabla_{\mathbf{W}}\ell_{\mathrm{CE}}) =∇𝐖A⋅Δ​𝐖Δ​α→∇𝐖A⋅d​𝐖d​α=d​Ad​α\displaystyle=\nabla_{\mathbf{W}}A\cdot\frac{\Delta\mathbf{W}}{\Delta\alpha}\to\nabla_{\mathbf{W}}A\cdot\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{W}}{\mathrm{d}\alpha}=\frac{\mathrm{d}A}{\mathrm{d}\alpha} (60)

Applying the chain rule once more for ∇𝐖ℓCE=(∇𝐖A)​d​ℓCEd​A\nabla_{\mathbf{W}}\ell_{\mathrm{CE}}=(\nabla_{\mathbf{W}}A)\frac{\mathrm{d}\ell_{\mathrm{CE}}}{\mathrm{d}A} (only AA depends on the weights) gives

d​Ad​α\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}A}{\mathrm{d}\alpha} =−η​dg​N​(∇𝐖A)2​d​ℓCEd​A\displaystyle=-\eta d_{g}N(\nabla_{\mathbf{W}}A)^{2}\frac{\mathrm{d}\ell_{\mathrm{CE}}}{\mathrm{d}A} (61)

when assuming the right-hand side is finite in the thermodynamic limit. It will be seen that this is indeed the case.

Define attention logits li​j=𝐪𝐢⊤​𝐤𝐣/dh=𝐖𝐐⊤​Ω​(j−i)​𝐖𝐊/dhl_{ij}=\mathbf{q_{i}^{\top}}\mathbf{k_{j}}/\sqrt{d_{h}}=\mathbf{W_{Q}^{\top}}\Omega(j-i)\mathbf{W_{K}}/\sqrt{d_{h}}. Then the gradient ∇𝐖A\nabla_{\mathbf{W}}A becomes

∇𝐖A\displaystyle\nabla_{\mathbf{W}}A =∑i=L+12​L∂A∂πi,i−L​∇𝐖πi,i−L=∑i=L+12​L∂A∂πi,i−L​∑k=1L∂πi,i−L∂li​k​∇𝐖li​k\displaystyle=\sum_{i=L+1}^{2L}\frac{\partial A}{\partial\pi_{i,i-L}}\,\nabla_{\mathbf{W}}\pi_{i,i-L}=\sum_{i=L+1}^{2L}\frac{\partial A}{\partial\pi_{i,i-L}}\sum_{k=1}^{L}\frac{\partial\pi_{i,i-L}}{\partial l_{ik}}\,\nabla_{\mathbf{W}}l_{ik} (62)

Let us define the function

c⁡(A)\displaystyle c(A) :=dg​N​(∇𝐖A)2=dg​N​[∑i,k=1L∂A∂πi+L,i​∂πi+L,i∂li+L,k​(∇𝐖li+L,k)]2\displaystyle:=d_{g}N(\nabla_{\mathbf{W}}A)^{2}=d_{g}N\Biggl[\sum_{i,k=1}^{L}\frac{\partial A}{\partial\pi_{i+L,i}}\frac{\partial\pi_{i+L,i}}{\partial l_{i+L,k}}\Bigl(\nabla_{\mathbf{W}}l_{i+L,k}\Bigr)\Biggr]^{2} (63)

then the differential equation reads

d​Ad​α\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}A}{\mathrm{d}\alpha} =η​c​(A)​11+1N−1​em⁡(A,R,S)​NN−1​dg−1dg​(R−S)\displaystyle=\eta\,c(A)\,\frac{1}{1+\frac{1}{N-1}\,\mathrm{e}^{m(A,R,S)}}\frac{N}{N-1}\frac{d_{g}-1}{d_{g}}(R-S) (64)

so that merely c⁡(A)c(A) needs to be yet determined. Given the derivatives

∂A∂πi+L,i\displaystyle\frac{\partial A}{\partial\pi_{i+L,i}} =1L\displaystyle=\frac{1}{L} (65)
∂πi+L,i∂li+L,k\displaystyle\frac{\partial\pi_{i+L,i}}{\partial l_{i+L,k}} =πi+L,i​(δi​k−πi+L,k)\displaystyle=\pi_{i+L,i}(\delta_{ik}-\pi_{i+L,k}) (66)
∇𝐖𝐐li+L,k\displaystyle\nabla_{\mathbf{W_{Q}}}l_{i+L,k} =Ω⁡(k−i−L)​𝐖𝐊dh\displaystyle=\frac{\Omega(k-i-L)\mathbf{W_{K}}}{\sqrt{d_{h}}} (67)
∇𝐖𝐊li+L,k\displaystyle\nabla_{\mathbf{W_{K}}}l_{i+L,k} =Ω⁡(i+L−k)​𝐖𝐐dh\displaystyle=\frac{\Omega(i+L-k)\mathbf{W_{Q}}}{\sqrt{d_{h}}} (68)

some linear algebra yields, for the approximation πi+L,j=A​δi​j+1−AL−1​(1−δi​j)\pi_{i+L,j}=A\delta_{ij}+\frac{1-A}{L-1}(1-\delta_{ij}) of an expected seed-averaged behavior,

c⁡(A)\displaystyle c(A) =dg​N​A2​(1−A)2​𝐖𝐊⊤​(𝕀−Λ)2​𝐖𝐊+𝐖𝐐⊤​(𝕀−Λ)2​𝐖𝐐dh\displaystyle=d_{g}NA^{2}(1-A)^{2}\frac{\mathbf{W_{K}^{\top}}(\mathbb{I}-\Lambda)^{2}\mathbf{W_{K}}+\mathbf{W_{Q}^{\top}}(\mathbb{I}-\Lambda)^{2}\mathbf{W_{Q}}}{d_{h}} (69)

where Λ=diag⁡(λ1,λ1,λ2,λ2,…,λdh/2,λdh/2)\Lambda=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{2},\dotsc,\lambda_{d_{h}/2},\lambda_{d_{h}/2}) with λn=1\lambda_{n}=1 for ωn∈2​π​ℤ\omega_{n}\in 2\pi\mathbb{Z} or otherwise

λn\displaystyle\lambda_{n} =1L−1​[1L​(sin⁡(ωn​L/2)sin⁡(ωn/2))2−1]\displaystyle=\frac{1}{L-1}\biggl[\frac{1}{L}\biggl(\frac{\sin(\omega_{n}L/2)}{\sin(\omega_{n}/2)}\biggr)^{2}-1\biggr] (70)

While the diagonal part in πi+L,j=A​δi​j+1−AL−1​(1−δi​j)\pi_{i+L,j}=A\delta_{ij}+\frac{1-A}{L-1}(1-\delta_{ij}) approximates the attention entries well, the off-diagonal entries behave differently during training. This elongates the smooth increase of AA in the learning regime. Without the uneven behavior, the slope of AA would grow too steeply, because A2​(1−A)2A^{2}(1-A)^{2} acts as a catalyst in the differential equation for AA. At the end of training, just as at the very beginning, this approximation describes the system well, however. Hence, the above expression for c⁡(A)c(A) may be used to determine the value at initialization, where the ansatz is still correct. We find that the empirical trajectory is approximated by c⁡(A)=L​cω⋅A⁡(1−A)c(A)=Lc_{\omega}\cdot A(1-A) with

cω\displaystyle c_{\omega} :=dg​NL​L−1L2​⟨𝐖𝐊⊤​(𝕀−Λ)2​𝐖𝐊+𝐖𝐐⊤​(𝕀−Λ)2​𝐖𝐐dh|α=0⟩𝐖𝐐,𝐖𝐊\displaystyle:=\frac{d_{g}N}{L}\,\frac{L-1}{L^{2}}\Biggl\langle\frac{\mathbf{W_{K}^{\top}}(\mathbb{I}-\Lambda)^{2}\mathbf{W_{K}}+\mathbf{W_{Q}^{\top}}(\mathbb{I}-\Lambda)^{2}\mathbf{W_{Q}}}{d_{h}}\Bigg|_{\alpha=0}\Biggr\rangle_{\mathbf{W_{Q}},\mathbf{W_{K}}} (71)

At initialization, 𝐖𝐐\mathbf{W_{Q}} and 𝐖𝐊\mathbf{W_{K}} are random vectors, such that, for some random 𝐗∈ℝdh\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{h}},

⟨𝐗⊤​(𝕀−Λ)2​𝐗⟩𝐗\displaystyle\langle\mathbf{X^{\top}}(\mathbb{I}-\Lambda)^{2}\mathbf{X}\rangle_{\mathbf{X}} =Tr⁡⟨𝐗⊤​(𝕀−Λ)2​𝐗⟩𝐗=Tr⁡[(𝕀−Λ)2​⟨𝐗⊤​𝐗⟩𝐗]\displaystyle=\Tr\langle\mathbf{X^{\top}}(\mathbb{I}-\Lambda)^{2}\mathbf{X}\rangle_{\mathbf{X}}=\Tr\Bigl[(\mathbb{I}-\Lambda)^{2}\langle\mathbf{X^{\top}}\mathbf{X}\rangle_{\mathbf{X}}\Bigr] (72)

exploiting the linearity of the trace and expectation value. ⟨𝐗𝐗⊤⟩𝐗\langle\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X^{\top}}\rangle_{\mathbf{X}} is the covariance matrix of 𝐗\mathbf{X}. An i.i.d. initialization yields a scaled unit matrix with, say, σ2\sigma^{2} as the variance. Then ⟨𝐗⊤​(𝕀−Λ)2​𝐗⟩𝐗=σ2​Tr⁡[(𝕀−Λ)2]\langle\mathbf{X^{\top}}(\mathbb{I}-\Lambda)^{2}\mathbf{X}\rangle_{\mathbf{X}}=\sigma^{2}\Tr\bigl[(\mathbb{I}-\Lambda)^{2}\bigr] and

cω\displaystyle c_{\omega} =dg​NL​L−1L2​σ2​2dh​Tr⁡[(𝕀−Λ)2]\displaystyle=\frac{d_{g}N}{L}\frac{L-1}{L^{2}}\,\sigma^{2}\frac{2}{d_{h}}\Tr\bigl[(\mathbb{I}-\Lambda)^{2}\bigr] (73)

Plugging in the definition of Λ\Lambda followed by some algebraic manipulations leads to the final expression in Eq. (14).

In principle, we can determine a discrete update step Δ​A\Delta A via a Taylor expansion in the Δ​li​j\Delta l_{ij} of the softmax activation. These, in turn, are expressible via Δ​𝐖𝐐,Δ​𝐖𝐊\Delta\mathbf{W_{Q}},\Delta\mathbf{W_{K}} resulting in a series in orders of the learning rate. The gradient-flow limit η→0\eta\to 0 lets these higher-order terms vanish. Small learning rates allow us to neglect them, yielding a first-order expression equivalent to the above derivative.

Appendix F Seed-averaged permutation matrix overlap

Our goal is to find the quantity Tr⁡[(Ma⋆)⊤​Mb⋆]\Tr\bigl[(M^{\star}_{a})^{\top}M^{\star}_{b}\bigr] for some a≠ba\neq b, a,b∈{1,…,dg}a,b\in\{1,\dotsc,d_{g}\} on average. Because a product of two permutation matrices is again a permutation matrix, we reduce the problem of finding the overlap of two random matrices by computing the average trace of a permutation. Thus, w.l.o.g., we can assume one of them to be the unit matrix. Since the trace is a linear operator, we can compute the average permutation matrix itself. As each entry in the first row has a probability of 1/N1/N to have a non-zero entry when constructing such a matrix, and because each row must behave alike due to symmetry, the average permutation matrix is filled with the entries 1/N1/N.

Now, we only want to consider overlaps of different permutation matrices, thus we have to consider only non-trivial matrices when assuming the other one is the identity. To account for that, we write

⟨M⋆⟩M⋆∈SN∖{𝕀N}\displaystyle\langle M^{\star}\rangle_{M^{\star}\in S^{N}\setminus\{\mathbb{I}_{N}\}} =1N!−1​(∑i=1N!Mi⋆−𝕀N)=1N!−1​(N!N​JN−𝕀N)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N!-1}\Biggl(\sum_{i=1}^{N!}M_{i}^{\star}-\mathbb{I}_{N}\Biggr)=\frac{1}{N!-1}\biggl(\frac{N!}{N}J_{N}-\mathbb{I}_{N}\biggr) (74)

with (JN)r​s=1(J_{N})_{rs}=1 ∀r,s=1,…,N\forall r,s=1,\dotsc,N and N≥2N\geq 2. Hence,

⟨Tr⁡M⋆⟩M⋆∈SN∖{𝕀N}\displaystyle\langle\Tr M^{\star}\rangle_{M^{\star}\in S^{N}\setminus\{\mathbb{I}_{N}\}} =N!N!−1−NN!−1=1−1(N−1)!1−1N!\displaystyle=\frac{N!}{N!-1}-\frac{N}{N!-1}=\frac{1-\frac{1}{(N-1)!}}{1-\frac{1}{N!}} (75)

With this intermediate finding, we may write

⟨Tr⁡[(Ma⋆)⊤​Mb⋆]⟩Ma⋆≠Mb⋆∈SN\displaystyle\Bigl\langle\Tr\Bigl[(M^{\star}_{a})^{\top}M^{\star}_{b}\Bigr]\Bigr\rangle_{M^{\star}_{a}\neq M^{\star}_{b}\in S^{N}} =1−1(N−1)!1−1N!\displaystyle=\frac{1-\frac{1}{(N-1)!}}{1-\frac{1}{N!}} (76)

when a≠ba\neq b. We immediately realize that this constant approaches 11 for N→+∞N\to+\infty. Therefore,

τ¯\displaystyle\overline{\tau} :=⟨τ⟩Ma⋆≠Mb⋆∈SN=1N​1−1(N−1)!1−1N!=1N−1N​N−1N!−1\displaystyle:=\langle\tau\rangle_{M^{\star}_{a}\neq M^{\star}_{b}\in S^{N}}=\frac{1}{N}\frac{1-\frac{1}{(N-1)!}}{1-\frac{1}{N!}}=\frac{1}{N}-\frac{1}{N}\frac{N-1}{N!-1} (77)

Appendix G Early training regime

At the start of training, AA remains on a plateau of A=A0A=A_{0}, which is 1/L1/L on average (every attention entry is equal with random key/query initializations). A Taylor expansion of the loss up to linear order describes the system well during the early training process. The differential equations are solvable exactly in this regime:

A⁡(α)=A0,R⁡(α)=η​N−1N​(A0+1−A0dg)⋅α,S⁡(α)=η​N−1N​1−A0dg⋅α\displaystyle A(\alpha)=A_{0}\ ,\qquad R(\alpha)=\eta\,\frac{N-1}{N}\biggl(A_{0}+\frac{1-A_{0}}{d_{g}}\biggr)\cdot\alpha\ ,\qquad S(\alpha)=\eta\,\frac{N-1}{N}\frac{1-A_{0}}{d_{g}}\cdot\alpha (78)

The matrix overlaps RR and SS increase linearly before higher-order terms in the loss become relevant and the attention mechanism starts to learn. We observe that the correct overlap increases faster than the overlap with wrong permutations.

Appendix H Onset of attention learning

In the main text, we observed initially a flat attention order parameter AA, followed by a rapid increase at the start of the second learning phase (see left panel of Fig. 2). Using this separation of learning into the two phases, we can analytically obtain an approximate solution of the differential equations for the order parameters that describe the onset of attention learning. Combining Eqs. (15b) and (15c), in the linearized regime of the first phase of training (Appendix G) where A⁡(0)=1/LA(0)=1/L, we find

d⁡(R−S)d​α\displaystyle\frac{{\rm d}(R-S)}{{\rm d}\alpha} ≈η​N−1N​1L.\displaystyle\approx\eta\,\frac{N-1}{N}\frac{1}{L}\ . (79)

In the limit of large NN, the solution is thus given by R−S≈α/LR-S\approx\alpha/L. Using this in the differential equation for the attention order parameter, Eq. (15a), yields, to leading order in 1/L1/L,

d​Ad​α\displaystyle\frac{{\rm d}A}{{\rm d}\alpha} ≈η2​cω​α​A\displaystyle\approx\eta^{2}c_{\omega}\alpha A (80)
⇒A⁡(α)\displaystyle\Rightarrow A(\alpha) ≈1L​exp⁡[cω2​η2​α2].\displaystyle\approx\frac{1}{L}\exp\left[\frac{c_{\omega}}{2}\eta^{2}\alpha^{2}\right]\ . (81)

This approximation is valid until the onset of the second learning phase. The timescale of the increase is set by 2/(cω​η)=O⁡(1)\sqrt{2/(c_{\omega}\eta)}=O(1).

Appendix I Final rollout accuracy modeling

To model the final rollout accuracy, we start with the recursion relation

P⁡(s^t+1=st+1)\displaystyle P(\hat{s}_{t+1}=s_{t+1}) =P⁡(s^t=st)⋅P⁡(s^t+1=st+1|s^t=st)\displaystyle=P(\hat{s}_{t}=s_{t})\cdot P(\hat{s}_{t+1}=s_{t+1}|\hat{s}_{t}=s_{t})
+[1−P(s^t=st)]⋅P(s^t+1=st+1|s^t≠st)\displaystyle\quad+\bigl[1-P(\hat{s}_{t}=s_{t})\bigr]\cdot P(\hat{s}_{t+1}=s_{t+1}|\hat{s}_{t}\neq s_{t}) (82)

with P⁡(s^0=s0)=1P(\hat{s}_{0}=s_{0})=1. We shorten the notation:

ϱt:=P⁡(s^t=st)𝒜t:=P⁡(s^t+1=st+1|s^t=st)ℬt:=P⁡(s^t+1=st+1|s^t≠st)\displaystyle\varrho_{t}:=P(\hat{s}_{t}=s_{t})\qquad\mathcal{A}_{t}:=P(\hat{s}_{t+1}=s_{t+1}|\hat{s}_{t}=s_{t})\qquad\mathcal{B}_{t}:=P(\hat{s}_{t+1}=s_{t+1}|\hat{s}_{t}\neq s_{t}) (83)

Then

ϱt+1\displaystyle\varrho_{t+1} =ϱt​(𝒜t−ℬt)+ℬt\displaystyle=\varrho_{t}(\mathcal{A}_{t}-\mathcal{B}_{t})+\mathcal{B}_{t} (84)

with ϱ0=1\varrho_{0}=1 for the initial token, and we seek ϱL\varrho_{L} from this recursion relation. It holds

ϱL\displaystyle\varrho_{L} =𝒜0​∏t=1L−1(𝒜t−ℬt)+∑t=1L−1[ℬt​∏i=t+1L−1(𝒜i−ℬi)]\displaystyle=\mathcal{A}_{0}\prod_{t=1}^{L-1}(\mathcal{A}_{t}-\mathcal{B}_{t})+\sum_{t=1}^{L-1}\Biggl[\mathcal{B}_{t}\prod_{i=t+1}^{L-1}(\mathcal{A}_{i}-\mathcal{B}_{i})\Biggr] (85)

The next state is chosen by the maximal argument of the logit vector. That is, 𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t} is the probability of choosing the correct logit (when operating on sts_{t}). From the definition of the logit, we see that the logit is the sts_{t}-th column of our action-conditioned map, which does not depend on the last state token st−1s_{t-1}. If we assume that the other logits are equally likely on average, and that the prediction of state ii behaves the same as that of state jj, then we may write

ℬt\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{t} ≈1−𝒜tN−1\displaystyle\approx\frac{1-\mathcal{A}_{t}}{N-1} (86)

Next, we need to find an expression for the probability of choosing the correct logit (given the current state is correct). For this, we model the correct logit as a Gaussian variable. A numerical check quickly supports this assumption: the correct logit is for different training examples and for each sequence step almost exactly distributed normally.

Viewing every sequence-step as the same, we can replace 𝒜t\mathcal{A}_{t} by 𝒜¯:=𝔼t∈[L]​[𝒜t]\overline{\mathcal{A}}:=\mathbb{E}_{t\in[L]}[\mathcal{A}_{t}] such that

ϱL\displaystyle\varrho_{L} ≈N−1N​(N​𝒜¯−1N−1)L+1N\displaystyle\approx\frac{N-1}{N}\biggl(\frac{N\overline{\mathcal{A}}-1}{N-1}\biggr)^{L}+\frac{1}{N} (87)

after some rearrangements and exploitation of a geometric sum with ∑n=0L−2rn=(1−rL−1)/(1−r)\sum_{n=0}^{L-2}r^{n}=(1-r^{L-1})/(1-r) and r=N​𝒜¯−1N−1r=\frac{N\overline{\mathcal{A}}-1}{N-1}. Here, the singularity is hit when 𝒜¯=1\overline{\mathcal{A}}=1, which cannot occur as the student is never able to achieve perfect predictions.

Immediately, we realize that ϱL→1\varrho_{L}\to 1 when 𝒜¯→1\overline{\mathcal{A}}\to 1. Random guessing (𝒜¯=1/N\overline{\mathcal{A}}=1/N) would yield ϱL=1/N\varrho_{L}=1/N – a random choice. Yet ϱL\varrho_{L} grows much slower: each token in the sequence has to be predicted correctly in a row.

The probability of the correct choice given the correct current logit can be expressed as

𝒜¯=P⁡(zk>maxf≠k⁡zf).\displaystyle\overline{\mathcal{A}}=P(z_{k}>\max_{f\neq k}z_{f}). (88)

This is equivalent to determining the probability of every other logit being at most xx (a certain correct logit zkz_{k}) and then integrating over xx including the Gaussian PDF of x=zkx=z_{k}:

𝒜¯\displaystyle\overline{\mathcal{A}} =∫−∞+∞d​x​e−(x−μk)2/(2σk2)2​π​σk​Φ​(x−μk¯σk¯)N−1\displaystyle=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\mathrm{d}x\,\frac{\mathrm{e}^{-(x-\mu_{k})^{2}/(2\sigma_{k}^{2})}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma_{k}}\,\Phi\!\biggl(\frac{x-\mu_{\overline{k}}}{\sigma_{\overline{k}}}\biggr)^{N-1} (89)

where Φ\Phi is the CDF of the Gaussian PDF:

Φ⁡(u):=∫−∞ud​y​e−y2/22​π\displaystyle\Phi(u):=\int_{-\infty}^{u}\mathrm{d}y\,\frac{\mathrm{e}^{-y^{2}/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}} (90)

Upon substituting u=(x−μk)/σku=(x-\mu_{k})/\sigma_{k}:

𝒜¯\displaystyle\overline{\mathcal{A}} =∫−∞+∞d​u​e−u2/22​π​Φ​(σkσk¯​u+μk−μk¯σk¯)N−1,\displaystyle=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}\mathrm{d}u\,\frac{\mathrm{e}^{-u^{2}/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\,\Phi\!\biggl(\frac{\sigma_{k}}{\sigma_{\overline{k}}}\,u+\frac{\mu_{k}-\mu_{\overline{k}}}{\sigma_{\overline{k}}}\biggr)^{N-1}, (91)
